newsitem.title: GERMANY: Blast damages Dresdner branch, not political.
newsitem.headline: Blast damages Dresdner branch, not political.

text.p: An explosive device badly damaged a branch of Dresdner Bank in western Germany on Monday, but police ruled out a political motive for the attack.

Police had been investigating whether steel workers angered by Dresdner's backing of a controversial corporate takeover bid had been behind the attack in the town of Hattingen, but said later they had found nothing to suggest such a connection.

The attackers had detonated the device in a night safe for after-hours cash deposits at the branch's entrance, police said. Much of the bank's glass entrance was shattered and the windows of buildings opposite were pockmarked by flying debris.

A police spokesman said witnesses had seen two men running away after the explosion in the entrance to the branch and it was possible they had been trying to get at cash deposited in the night safe. He said they escaped empty-handed.
Trade unions sharply criticised Dresdner Bank last week because its investment banking unit was helping to finance a hostile takeover bid for steel firm Thyssen by rival Krupp.

The Thyssen workers' council and the metals and engineering union IG Metall condemned the explosion as a "brutal act of terror" and said the goal of its protest was not to endanger life or damage property.
The takeover was expected to cost thousands of jobs in Germany's steel-and-coal Ruhr Valley heartland and prompted a wave of outrage and industrial stoppages.

The uproar that followed the announcement of Krupp's takeover plans prompted the company to say it would hold talks with Thyssen to see if they could increase their cooperation in steel to avert an all-out hostile takeover.
Police said the attack in Hattingen, which is close to the city of Essen where Krupp has its headquarters, occurred at 4.16 a.m. (0316 GMT).
